id: [Were it but Me that gained the Height—]

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

World like a coat, silver clasps, ermine lined, warm with the dead inside, rolling around in the red center—I thought everything had a purpose—this was back when I still drank—and wasn’t I a special traveler, nestled in that pocket amongst the butterscotch candies, the matchbooks? Unessential but accounted for, a steady thing to touch. World like a morning glory, withered every evening, world like a bristling dog, terrified of thunder—I can’t believe how I believed, or how that belief assumed a shape around my body, taking on the imprint of my heat, gaining solidity. When anyone questioned me, I held it forth, let them touch the sleeve—I needed nothing. World like an egret, still and white on the highway divider, world like a regret typed out and then erased—I cannot hold you any closer without everyone seeing, I cannot hold you at all, it seems, your evergreens, your curling potato vine; it’s all too much much, and I a bit of goosedown, a thistle fluff, naked and hatless, unaccounted for and extra, the world like a world like a world.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker recalls a past state, associated with drinking, when they believed the world had purpose and that they occupied a meaningful, cared-for place within it.
- Using shifting metaphors, the speaker portrays the world as both comforting and fragile, capable of withering, trembling, or vanishing like an egret or an erased regret.
- The speaker describes how their belief once took on physical solidity, becoming a garment they could display to others as proof of their self-sufficiency.

outputs.L1: World like a coat—silver clasps, ermine-lined, warm with the dead within, tumbling about in that red core—I once believed everything had its purpose. This was back when I still drank. And was I not a singular traveler, nestled in that pocket among the butterscotch candies and matchbooks? Inessential, yet accounted for—a constant thing to touch. outputs.L2: The universe fit me like an overcoat—clasped in silver, lined with ermine, kept warm by the corpses tucked within, tumbling through its crimson heart. Back in my drinking days, I imagined that all things served some function—and didn't I feel like a chosen passenger, tucked snug in that pocket beside the butterscotch sweets and the matchbooks? Not needed, yet still counted, a solid thing my fingers could find. The universe was a morning glory that shriveled at dusk, a trembling hound cowering from the storm's noise—I'm astonished now at the depth of my faith, at how that conviction molded itself against my form, absorbing the shape of my warmth, hardening into something real. Whenever someone doubted me, I offered it up, invited them to feel the sleeve—I lacked for nothing. The universe was an egret, motionless and pale upon the roadway median, a piece of remorse keyed onto a page and then deleted—I can't draw you nearer without every eye upon us, and honestly it seems I can't embrace you whatsoever: your pines, your twisting potato vines. It's simply far too overwhelming, and here I am, mere goose down, a wisp of thistle, bare-headed and exposed, uncounted and left over, the universe like a universe like a universe.
outputs.L3:
# Reflections on a Lost Certainty

There was a time, bound up with the ritual of drinking, when I believed the world was ordered by purpose. In those days I felt certain that existence itself intended something, and that I occupied a place within it—a meaningful place, one where I was held, accounted for, and cared for by the vast machinery of things. To live was to belong, and to belong was to be assured that nothing about my presence was accidental.

The world, as I understood it then, was tender toward me, yet even in my certainty I sensed its fragility. It comforted me the way a warm room comforts, and yet it seemed always on the verge of thinning into nothing. It could wither like a flower closing at dusk, or tremble like something startled, or vanish altogether—lifting away as suddenly as an egret takes flight from the shallows, or dissolving as cleanly as a regret one has finally learned to erase. It was at once my shelter and the most delicate thing I knew.

For a while, this belief hardened into something I could hold. My conviction acquired a strange solidity, becoming almost a garment I could wear. I draped it about myself and displayed it to others, offering it as evidence that I needed nothing more, that I was whole and self-sufficient, clothed in the certainty of my own belonging.

But that certainty has since come undone. It slipped from me and dissolved, and in its absence I find I can no longer take hold of the world. Its beauty pours out endlessly, its abundance overflows on every side, and I stand unable to gather any of it into my arms. What once felt like an embrace now escapes my grasp entirely; I cannot hold what I once believed was holding me.

And so I am left weightless, stripped of the garment that once defined me. I feel exposed, unaccounted for, no longer named or noticed by anything larger than myself. I have become a small and fragile scrap, drifting without anchor through a world that has been emptied of its clear meaning—light enough to be carried off by any wind, and belonging, now, to nothing at all.
outputs.L4:
# The Fragile Architecture of Belief

There was a time when the speaker moved through the world as though it were something that could be held—cupped in the hands like water, cradled like an egg, wrapped around the shoulders like a coat against the cold. In those days, belief came easily. It arrived, perhaps, with the warmth of drink, that loosening of the mind that made everything feel purposeful and protected. The world seemed then to be a comforting thing, soft-edged and generous, a place that returned the speaker's trust with a sense of belonging.

The poem builds itself through these shifting metaphors, each one offering the world as some tender, breakable object. It is comforting, yes—but always fragile. The coat can be shed. The egg can crack. The water, no matter how carefully held, slips through the fingers and is gone. In this way, the poem quietly warns us that the very things which console us are the things most likely to fail. Certainty, like faith, is beautiful precisely because it cannot last.

And so the speaker's belief begins to dissolve. The drinking that once accompanied conviction now appears in a different light—not as a source of transcendence but as a fragile scaffolding, a temporary structure that could not bear the weight placed upon it. What once gave purpose and protection is revealed as illusion, a story the speaker told themselves in order to feel safe.

By the poem's close, that safety has fallen away entirely. The speaker stands "naked and hatless, unaccounted for"—stripped of the coverings that once shielded them, no longer counted, no longer sure of their place in any larger order. This is the state of disillusionment: not merely sadness, but exposure. To lose one's comforting certainties is to be laid bare before a world that will not be held, that resists the grasping hand and the cradling arm.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that such vulnerability may be the truest condition of being. The world was never something to be possessed or fully understood; it only appeared that way through the softening lens of faith and drink. When those illusions collapse, what remains is the raw and unaccommodated self, standing hatless in the open, face to face with a reality that offers no easy comfort—and asks, instead, to be met without protection.
outputs.L5:
# When the World Feels Unessential

There are moments in life when the entire **world** seems to fade into the background, when the noise of daily obligations quiets down and everything that once felt urgent suddenly appears **unessential**.

**When** we pause to reflect, we often realize how much of what we chase is not truly necessary. The endless pursuit of possessions, status, and approval can consume our days, yet it rarely brings lasting fulfillment. So much of what the modern **world** demands of us is, in the end, **unessential** to living a meaningful life.

## Recognizing What Truly Matters

It is easy to get lost in the constant motion of the **world** around us. Every notification, every deadline, every trend competes for our attention. But **when** we step back and ask ourselves what genuinely matters, the answer is often simpler than we expect: connection, health, purpose, and peace of mind.

The things we label as important are frequently **unessential** when viewed from a broader perspective. Consider how differently we value our time **when** facing a challenge or a loss. Suddenly, the small worries that once dominated our thoughts reveal themselves as trivial.

## Finding Clarity

The key is not to reject the **world**, but to engage with it more thoughtfully. **When** we learn to distinguish the essential from the **unessential**, we free ourselves to live with greater intention and joy.

In the quiet spaces between our busy hours, we can rediscover what a rich and balanced life truly looks like—one where the **unessential** falls away, and the **world** becomes a place of meaning rather than mere distraction.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem that uses the repeating phrase "world like a..." with a series of vivid, unexpected similes, exploring the loss of faith or certainty.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains

The world like a coat I once believed would keep me warm, now threadbare at the elbows where I leaned too hard on things.

The world like a house whose rooms I memorized in darkness, only to find, at dawn, the doors had all been painted on.

I used to pray. The words came easy then, like water finding its own level, like a child's hand reaching up and always meeting the hand it expected. Now the world like a phone still pressed to my ear long after the line went dead—that patient, foolish listening for a voice that isn't coming.

The world like a map of a country that has since changed all its borders. The world like a language I spoke fluently in a dream and cannot recall on waking, only the ache of having known.

They told me certainty was solid ground. But the world like a frozen lake in April—still walkable, still holding, until it isn't. The world like a photograph left in sun, the faces going pale, then paler, then only the light where faces were.

And still I rise. And still I move through the hours. The world like a song I've forgotten the meaning of but hum anyway, because my mouth remembers what my heart let go. The world like a lantern I carry into rooms that may be empty, may be full—I cannot say, I only know I keep lifting it, keep looking, the small flame trembling in my hands like something almost, almost like a prayer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness piece about someone who once believed the world had a purpose and now feels unaccounted for and adrift.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ledger of Unaccounting

There was a time I kept my faith like coins in a jar, each one minted with a face I trusted—*this happens because,* and *that arrives for,* and every falling thing fell toward some waiting hand.

I believed. Oh, how I believed the way a river believes in the sea, never doubting the ground would slope forever downward toward some gathering, some arms, some reason wearing my name like a coat tailored before I was born.

And now—

Now the slope has gone level. Now the water pools and forgets which way is home. I am standing in the middle of a sentence that has lost its verb, and no one comes to finish it, no one leans down to say *ah yes, here is where you were needed all along.*

Where did it go, the purpose? Did I misplace it like a set of keys, will I find it in some pocket of an old year, some coat I've stopped wearing? Or was it never there, was it only the shape my wanting pressed into the fog, a face I saw in the wallpaper that dissolves the moment I stop needing it to be a face?

I was going to *matter.* The word sits in my mouth now like a stone I can neither swallow nor spit out. To matter—to have mass, to have weight, to bend the world however slightly toward the fact of me. And instead I am a smoke of a person, drifting where the draft decides, unaccounted, un-tallied, missing from every ledger, a debt no one is trying to collect because no one wrote me down.

And still—

*and still*—

the mornings come. Look at them come, indifferent and gold, not for me, not against me, simply *come,* the way rain doesn't hate the field or love it. And there is something almost merciful in that indifference, some cold water I could learn to drink. If nothing means, then nothing *demands.* If I am adrift, then I am also *free* of the harbor that never existed, free to invent a small warmth, a made thing, a purpose stitched by my own hands from whatever thread is left—

not found, then.

*Made.*

Perhaps that is the whole of it. Perhaps the arms I waited for were always my own, folding at last around this drifting, unaccounted, still-breathing thing I am—

and calling it, quietly,

*enough.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a contemporary poet like Mary Ruefle—dense, associative imagery, dashes, and a melancholy meditation on belief and belonging.
counterfactuals.output:
# Article of Faith

I believed in the door—
its brass knob worn to a moon
by hands that wanted out, or in,
I could never tell which hunger
polishes a thing.

There is a country
where the dead keep their coats on.
I have applied for citizenship
three times. Each time the form asks
*what did you love and did it love you back*—
and I leave the second part blank,
the way you leave a light on
for no one.

Belonging is a kind of weather.
It arrives without asking,
it leaves the same—
and in between, the small
administrations of grief:
a spoon, a chair pulled out,
the way my mother folded envelopes
as if sealing something in
that might otherwise
have escaped and lived.

I wanted to believe.
I practiced on the smaller gods first—
the god of the misplaced key,
the god of almost-said—
before attempting the enormous ones,
the ones who don't answer
because they are busy
being everywhere at once,
which is another word for gone.

Once I was so lonely
I confessed to a window.
It gave nothing back but my own face
laid over the street,
the two of us
transparent,
each pretending
to be the more real.

And still the door.
And still the brass moon
warming under a stranger's grip.
I have decided
faith is what you keep doing
after you've stopped—
the way a bell,
struck once,
goes on
being struck
inside itself
long after
the sound
has agreed
to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem that begins by comparing the world to a coat and ends with the phrase "the world like a world like a world."
counterfactuals.output:
**COAT**

The world like a coat you put on backwards, the buttons pressing their cold moons into your spine. Someone left the sleeves inside out, someone stitched the weather into the lining. You reach for a pocket and find another pocket and inside that, the smell of a season that hasn't been invented.

I wore it to the wedding. I wore it to the drowning. It fit the way a name fits a stranger, which is to say it hung on me, a rumor of shoulders.

Consider the buttons: each one a small planet refusing to be fastened. Consider the collar, turned up against a wind that comes from *inside* the cloth. There is no outside. That is the first lesson of the coat. There is no taking it off, and this is the second, and they contradict, and both are worn at once like two coats, like a coat over a coat, like a body learning it was always only weather.

Here is a thread. Pull it. Watch the sleeve unspool into a road, the road into a river of gray yarn, the river into a single strand a spider might use to lower itself, thinking, *ah, the ground,* thinking, *ah, at last,* and finding only more coat, more lining, more of the borrowed heat we mistake for our own.

They asked me what I was wearing and I said the century. They asked again and I said everyone I have ever touched, sewn edge to edge, a quilt pretending to be a garment pretending to be a life.

Take it off, they said. Take it off, take it off—

but the arms are the arms, and the buttons are the small refusing moons, and under the coat is the coat, and under that

the world like a world like a world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of literary writing about faith, alcoholism, and the fragile shape our beliefs take around our bodies, using surreal metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cartography of Emptied Glasses

My grandmother believed in God the way water believes in the shape of its container. On Sundays she poured herself into the pew, took the form of devotion, and by Monday she had leaked out again, seeking lower ground.

I learned faith from her trembling hands.

There was a bottle in our house that contained the ocean. This is not a metaphor, or it is only a metaphor, which is the same thing when you are seven and watching your father drink the tide out of a glass. Each swallow lowered the water somewhere in the world. Each swallow raised it behind his eyes, until he was drowning standing up, until he was a lighthouse with the light turned inward, warning ships away from the rocks of his own ribcage.

*Believe in me,* he'd say, and I did, the way you believe in weather.

---

Faith is the fragile architecture we build around the animal of the body. I understand this now. We are all housing something that wants to escape—the way steam wants to escape the kettle, the way prayer wants to escape the mouth, the way the amber liquid wanted to escape my father and take him with it, evaporating him one evening at a time until he was just an outline where a man had been standing.

The church taught me the body was a temple.

The bottle taught me the temple could be emptied and still charge admission.

---

Here is what nobody tells you: belief is a substance you can pour. It has viscosity. It clings to the sides of whatever holds it. My mother held her faith like she held her breath—a thing done in defiance, a thing that turned her blue at the edges, a thing she released only in the dark when she thought no one could measure the color of her surrender.

She prayed over him. She prayed the way you might pray over a garden planted in salt: with hope embarrassed by its own foolishness, with love that had learned to grow in impossible soil.

*God is a fisherman,* she told me. *He is patient. He will pull us up eventually.*

But we were the fish who had learned to love the hook. We were the congregation of the thirsty, kneeling at an altar that dispensed forgetting instead of grace.

---

I found my father's faith once, folded in the drawer beside his bed. It had the texture of a receipt—proof of a transaction, faded past reading. He had traded something for something. The exchange rate was cruel. The currency was years.

When I drink now—and I do drink now, the inheritance flowing down through generations like a river that refuses to forget its source—I feel the old shape trying to fill me. The container remembers what it was made to hold.

I am my grandmother's granddaughter. I take the form of whatever pours into me.

Some nights that is grief. Some nights that is the ghost of a God I can neither keep nor abandon. Some nights it is the bottle's ocean, rising, and I am seven again, watching the tide go out of someone I love, understanding at last that faith and thirst are the same hunger wearing different clothes.

---

We believe because we are empty and cannot bear it.

We drink because we are empty and cannot bear it.

The tragedy is not that these are different.

The tragedy is that they are the same reaching—two hands cupped toward the same absent water, two mouths shaped around the same silent name, two bodies learning that whatever we are built to contain, we are also built to lose.

My grandmother died in the shape of her belief. My father is dying in the shape of his thirst.

And I—I am still deciding which vessel I will become, still standing at the confluence where the sacred and the ruinous pour from the same wounded sky, still trying to learn the difference between a prayer and a plea, between communion and consumption, between the wine that saves and the wine that empties us out onto the floor of our own cathedral, gasping, luminous, and terribly, holily alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
